:::{#def-lbfgs}
#### Limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS)

**Limited-memory BFGS** (**L-BFGS**)
[@nocedal2006numerical, Chapter 7]
is the [quasi-Newton method](#def-quasi-newton-method)
that never forms $\matr{H}^{(t)}$.
It stores only the $m$ most recent pairs $(\vecf{s}^{(j)}, \vy^{(j)})$,
with $m$ small, such as $5$ or $20$,
and obtains $\matr{H}^{(t)} \deriv{\vx} f(\vx^{(t)})$
implicitly, through a few vector operations,
as if the [BFGS update](#def-bfgs-update) for those $m$ pairs were applied
to a simple starting [matrix](linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matrix), such as a multiple of $\matr{I}_p$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-lbfgs-step}
#### L-BFGS applies the update without forming the matrix

Continue @exm-bfgs-step with $m = 1$ stored pair $(\vecf{s}^{(0)}, \vy^{(0)})$ and starting [matrix](linear-algebra-matrices.qmd#def-matrix) $\matr{I}_2$.
Below, $\matr{H}^+ \deriv{\vx} f(\vx^{(1)})$ is formed from vectors alone, in two passes over the stored pair,
then compared with the [matrix product](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-mult).

```{r}
#| label: lbfgs-step
#| code-fold: false
g1 <- grad(x1)
alpha <- rho * sum(s * g1)
r <- g1 - alpha * y
beta <- rho * sum(y * r)
r <- r + s * (alpha - beta)
rbind(from_vectors = r, from_matrix = drop(H1 %*% g1))
```

The two rows agree to within `{r} format(max(abs(r - H1 %*% g1)), digits = 2)`, although the first never forms the matrix.
BFGS stores a dense $p \times p$ matrix and spends about $p^2$ operations per iteration;
L-BFGS stores $2m$ vectors with $p$ entries and spends about $m p$ operations per iteration, so it remains usable when $p$ is in the millions.

:::
